realism_constraints: No modern forensic DNA or electronic surveillance
Medical jurisprudence and X-ray photography are emerging sciences
Legal procedures require physical evidence and witness testimony
institution: British Museum; Probate Court; Coroner's Court; Police
crime_subtype: body substitution with an Egyptian mummy

cast.private_secret: keen investigator of the Bellingham case

cast.name: Paul Berkeley
cast.private_secret: involved in the investigation and personal affairs

cast.name: Godfrey Bellingham
cast.role_archetype: impecunious gentleman and brother of victim

cast.name: Ruth Bellingham
cast.private_secret: deeply involved in family mystery and personal feelings

cast.name: Arthur Jellicoe
cast.private_secret: murderer of John Bellingham and manipulator of evidence

opportunity_channels: access to John Bellingham's house and mummy

surface_summary: John Bellingham mysteriously disappears after last being seen at his solicitor's office. Human remains are found scattered in various locations, suggesting murder. The will's complicated burial clause causes legal disputes over inheritance.
accepted_facts: Human remains matching his description were found dismembered in Kent and Essex.
A defective will made inheritance conditional on burial in a specific parish.
An Egyptian mummy was presented to the British Museum from Bellingham's collection.
inferred_conclusions: John Bellingham left voluntarily and is alive in hiding.
Godfrey Bellingham or his daughter Ruth murdered John Bellingham.
The dismembered remains found are those of John Bellingham.
mechanism_description: Arthur Jellicoe murdered John Bellingham accidentally by causing him to fall down the stairs. He concealed the body by substituting it with an Egyptian mummy from Bellingham's collection. Jellicoe manipulated the will and evidence to secure the estate but was ultimately exposed by Thorndyke's investigation and committed suicide.
delivery_path: Jellicoe causes Bellingham's accidental death by pushing him down stairs.
Jellicoe embalms and prepares Bellingham's body as a mummy.
He substitutes the mummy for the real body in Bellingham's house.
Jellicoe disposes of the real mummy's remains in various locations to mislead investigators.
He fabricates evidence including a personation at Hurst's house to fix disappearance date.
Thorndyke investigates, uses X-ray photography to identify the mummy as Bellingham's body.
Jellicoe is confronted and commits suicide by cyanide poisoning.
outcome_result: The true cause of John Bellingham's death and the substitution of his body with a mummy are revealed, and the culprit, Arthur Jellicoe, dies by suicide.

false_assumption.statement: John Bellingham was last seen alive at Hurst's house on November 23, 1902.
false_assumption.why_it_seems_reasonable: The housemaid at Hurst's house reported seeing a man claiming to be Bellingham there on that date. The presence of a scarab associated with Bellingham was found on the grounds.
false_assumption.what_it_hides: The man seen was an impersonator, and Bellingham was last seen alive weeks earlier at his own house, where he died.

supporting_points: The scarab was found on his property.
He had a motive related to inheritance.
He refused a financial arrangement proposed by Hurst.
He was present at the house when the visitor disappeared.
false_solution.the_one_flaw: No evidence that he had opportunity or that the visitor was actually Bellingham.

red_herrings.description: A scarab belonging to John Bellingham was found on the grounds of Godfrey Bellingham's house, suggesting his presence there.
red_herrings.innocent_explanation: The scarab was dropped by the real culprit, Jellicoe, to mislead suspicion.

red_herrings.description: Dismembered human remains were found in a watercress-bed and other ponds, suggesting a violent murder.
red_herrings.innocent_explanation: The remains were parts of the substituted mummy, not the real body.

closed_circle.rationale: The disappearance and murder involved only these family members and the solicitor, as established by the will, property, and last known movements.

time_anchors: October 14, 1902 - last confirmed sighting of John Bellingham
November 23, 1902 - alleged sighting at Hurst's house
July 15, 1904 - discovery of dismembered arm in watercress-bed
time_windows: Between October 14 and November 23, 1902 - time of disappearance
Two years after disappearance - period before presumption of death
access_actors: Arthur Jellicoe - access to Bellingham's house and mummy
Godfrey Bellingham - access to family property
George Hurst - access to his own house
access_objects: Watercress-bed and ponds in Kent and Essex
trust_channels: Solicitor-client relationship between Jellicoe and John Bellingham

inference_path.observation: John Bellingham was last seen alive on October 14, 1902, at his house.
inference_path.correction: The supposed later sighting on November 23 was an impersonation.
inference_path.effect: The disappearance date is earlier than initially believed.
required_evidence: Testimony of Dr. Norbury and Mr. Jellicoe about last meeting with Bellingham
Housemaid's statement denying presence of Bellingham on November 23

inference_path.observation: Dismembered human remains found in watercress-bed and ponds.
inference_path.correction: The remains are parts of an Egyptian mummy, not a recent body.
inference_path.effect: The remains do not belong to John Bellingham.
required_evidence: X-ray photographs of the mummy showing dental fillings matching Bellingham's dentist records
Medical examination of bones showing no signs of recent injury

inference_path.observation: The third finger of the left hand is missing from the remains.
inference_path.correction: The finger was removed after death to conceal identity.
inference_path.effect: The removal was deliberate to mislead identification.
required_evidence: Medical testimony on bone condition of finger
Knowledge of Bellingham's ring fitting tightly on that finger

inference_path.observation: A scarab belonging to Bellingham was found on the grounds of Godfrey Bellingham's house.
inference_path.correction: The scarab was planted by the murderer to mislead suspicion.
inference_path.effect: Suspicion on Godfrey Bellingham is unfounded.
required_evidence: Timing and location of scarab discovery
Presence of Arthur Jellicoe at the scene

inference_path.observation: The will contains a burial clause making inheritance conditional.
inference_path.correction: The clause was deliberately exploited by Jellicoe to manipulate inheritance.
inference_path.effect: Jellicoe had motive to murder and conceal the body.
required_evidence: Copy of the will certified by Godfrey Bellingham
Testimony of Mr. Marchmont and legal analysis

inference_path.observation: Mummy was delivered to the British Museum after Bellingham's disappearance.
inference_path.correction: The mummy contains the real body of John Bellingham.
inference_path.effect: The body was substituted to conceal the murder.
required_evidence: X-ray photographs identifying dental fillings and surgical wires
Tattoo of Eye of Osiris matching Bellingham's tattoo

inference_path.observation: Arthur Jellicoe was last person to see Bellingham alive and had access to mummy.
inference_path.correction: Jellicoe murdered Bellingham and concealed the body in the mummy.
required_evidence: Medical and forensic evidence from Thorndyke's investigation

discriminating_test.design: Thorndyke used X-ray photography to examine the mummy presented to the British Museum, revealing dental fillings and surgical repairs matching John Bellingham's medical records, confirming the identity of the body inside the mummy case.
discriminating_test.knowledge_revealed: The test revealed that the mummy contained the real body of John Bellingham, proving the substitution and implicating Jellicoe.
discriminating_test.pass_condition: The X-ray photograph must show dental and surgical features matching Bellingham's known medical history.

fair_play_explanation: The reader is given detailed descriptions of the will, the timeline of disappearances, the discovery of remains, and the peculiarities of the mummy. Clues such as the missing finger, the tight ring, the timing of the mummy's delivery, and the legal complications are all presented. The reader could deduce the substitution and the involvement of the solicitor by carefully analyzing these facts.
